newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FOCUS-S.Africa's Stals bullish on growth in 1997.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-S.Africa's Stals bullish on growth in 1997.

text.p: South Africa's economy could grow by close to three percent in 1997, confounding pessimists who expected a marked slowdown this year, Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals said on Tuesday.
"It is quite possible that the growth rate of the gross domestic production can be maintained at a level not very far below three percent for this year," he said in an interview with Reuters.
Real gross domestic product increased by 3.1 percent in 1996, slightly down from the 3.4 percent seen in 1995.
Stals said most economists at the start of the year, including those at the Reserve Bank, had been looking for a slowdown in real GDP in 1997 to around 2.0 to 2.5 percent.
But recent data from the fourth quarter of 1996 and the early months of 1997 suggested the economy was performing more strongly than expected.

South Africa's manufacturing industry, in particular, has been given a boost by a jump in exports, stimulated by the depreciation of the rand which lost a fifth of its value against a basket of currencies in 1996.

"It is not impossible that the motivation of the export industries because of the devaluation of last year can boost the growth rate in the economy, and maybe the total real economic production of 1997 will not be much below the performances of the last two years," Stals said.

At the same time, gross domestic expenditure should not increase by more than around three percent in 1997, keeping the economy in equilbrium and cutting the deficit on the current account of the balance of payments, he said.
"If that works out there is no reason why the current account of the balance of payments should provide any problems in 1997," Stals said.

He noted there had already been a marked improvement, with the seasonally adjusted and annualised deficit on the current account falling from 16 billion rand ($3.6 billion) in the second quarter of last year to eight billion in the third quarter and four billion in the fourth quarter.
Stals said he expected the deficit to hold below five billion rand in 1997.
That, in turn, should help to stabilise the rand.

He noted this year's appreciation meant the rand had fallen by a net 16 percent against a basket of currencies in the last 14 months -- roughly equivalent to two years' worth of inflation differentials between South Africa and its major trading partners.
"If we've had 16 percent over the last 14 months we have used up the 'quota' for 1997 and 1996," he said.

"I think the exchange rate has adjusted itself through market forces back to fundamentals, to the inflation differentials. And it is for that reason that we believe that in 1997 we will see a much more stable foreign exchange market."
Next week's South African budget should reassure sceptical markets that the government is committed to economic reform and structural adjustment, Stals added.

"Without knowing what will be in the budget in detail, I am sure that it will confirm again to the market that the South African government is able and determined to implement the structural adjustments necessary to raise the growth potential of the economy to higher levels."
Finance Minister Trevor Manuel presents his 1997/98 budget to parliament on March 12.
